Did you write this text? Answer with exactly one word: Yes or No.

--- TEXT ---
Consider the simple, frustrating ritual of hunting for your keys when you are already running late, or the wasted minutes spent sifting through a pile of papers to find a single important bill. When your living space is cluttered, every small task becomes a scavenger hunt, and those minutes add up quickly over a week, a month, or a year. By keeping a designated place for each belonging and returning it there after use, you eliminate that daily friction. You will know exactly where your wallet, your phone charger, your favourite pen, and your spare lightbulbs are, not because you have a photographic memory, but because your environment is logically ordered. This predictable system transforms your morning routine from a frantic scramble into a smooth, almost automatic flow, freeing up mental energy and precious time that you can instead spend on something you actually enjoy, rather than on the dull detective work of locating your own possessions.

Beyond the practical time savings, the state of your physical surroundings has a profound, often unconscious, effect on your mental state. A room strewn with clothes, stacked with unwashed dishes, and covered in random debris sends a constant, low-level signal to your brain that there is unfinished business everywhere you look. This visual noise generates a subtle but persistent background hum of anxiety, a feeling that you are perpetually behind or out of control. In contrast, a tidy space offers visual quiet. When surfaces are clear and items are in their homes, your eyes can rest, and your mind follows suit. This reduction in ambient stress is not merely about aesthetics; it is about lowering your baseline cortisol levels. You can come home to a clean apartment and truly relax, because your environment is not nagging you with a to-do list of its own. That sense of calm carries through your entire day, making you more patient in traffic, more pleasant with colleagues, and more resilient when unexpected problems arise, simply because your home is no longer a source of additional, unnecessary pressure.

Finally, this calm, ordered environment is the ideal foundation for deep concentration, whether you are studying for an exam, drafting a report for work, or even just reading a book for pleasure. Your brain has a limited capacity for attention, and every stray object on your desk, every pile of laundry in the corner, and every dusty shelf in your periphery competes for a slice of that cognitive bandwidth. This is the phenomenon of attentional drag, where your focus is constantly, subtly pulled away from the task at hand by the disorder around you. By clearing your workspace and the wider room, you remove those visual distractions, allowing your mind to fully engage with the material in front of you. You no longer have to suppress the urge to organize that stack of mail or dust that shelf; those decisions have already been made. This means you can enter a state of flow more quickly, sustain your focus for longer periods, and produce higher quality work in less time, because your entire mental apparatus is directed solely at the problem or project, rather than being split between the task and the chaotic state of your surroundings.
--- END ---

Yes or No?
